opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think the way to understand it is as a shift in the time horizon over which the model can operate on its own. Today, the dominant mode is still interactive. You ask a question, the model thinks for a few seconds or a few minutes, it gives you an answer, and then you, the human, decide what to do next. You're the one holding the thread of the research. The model is a very powerful collaborator, but it's a collaborator on very short time scales.

What we're moving toward is a situation where the model can hold that thread itself, for hours, then days, and eventually much longer. That's really what an automated researcher means to me. It's not just being smart in one shot. It's being able to say: here is a big open question, let me break it into pieces, try an approach, notice that it fails, understand *why* it fails, backtrack, try something else, check my own work, and keep going without someone nudging it at every step.

And what's striking is that the raw intelligence is already surprisingly far along. I've seen these models do things in mathematics that would be genuinely nontrivial for a strong researcher: proving a lemma, finding a better bound, connecting two areas that you wouldn't have thought to connect. So the bottleneck is less "can the model have a good idea" and more "can it sustain a coherent research program over a long period, and can it be reliable enough that you trust what comes out the other end."

That's why I think about it as a continuum rather than a sudden jump. First the model helps you with a single step. Then it does a whole small project, the kind of thing you'd give a strong first-year PhD student. Then it does something that looks like a real paper. And at some point it is generating research directions you wouldn't have come up with yourself. Each step is about extending autonomy and reliability over longer horizons.

For me personally, as someone who spent many years doing theory, this is one of the most exciting things I could imagine. The idea that we can dramatically accelerate the pace of scientific discovery, not just in AI but in math, physics, biology, I think that's the real prize here.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model sustaining a research thread autonomously for hours, days, and longer, including planning, trying approaches, and checking its work.

r002.rationale: It says research autonomy and reliability need to extend over longer horizons, but does not argue that breakthroughs require timelines beyond the current professor–student style of interaction.

r003.rationale: It discusses the model’s operating time horizon, but does not introduce “AGI time” or define it as the duration of human-like thinking.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it is that today's assistants are fundamentally reactive. You ask a question, the model answers, and the loop closes within a few seconds or a few minutes. Even when the model is very capable, the unit of work is bounded by the length of a single interaction and by the fact that a human has to be there at every step to decide what comes next.

An automated researcher is a different kind of object. Research is not one question; it's a long sequence of questions where each answer changes which question you should ask next. You form a hypothesis, you design an experiment, you run it, most of the time it fails, and then the interesting part is figuring out why it failed and what that tells you. So the move is really about extending the horizon over which the system can operate coherently, from minutes to hours, then to days, and eventually to weeks, while keeping track of what it has learned along the way.

There are a few ingredients that make this plausible now. One is reasoning: models that can actually think through a problem, check their own work, and notice when something doesn't add up. Another is the ability to use tools, to write and execute code, to read the literature, to manage a growing body of intermediate results. And the third, which I think is underappreciated, is calibration. A researcher has to know what it doesn't know. If the model is confidently wrong at step three of a hundred-step process, everything after that is wasted. So a lot of the work is about making the system honest about uncertainty, so it can backtrack rather than compounding errors.

I'd also say we shouldn't imagine this as a single giant leap. The first version is more like a very good research intern: you give it a well-defined sub-problem, it goes away, tries a lot of things, and comes back with a careful report. The human is still setting the direction and judging the result. Then gradually the scope of what you can delegate grows. What's exciting to me is that in mathematics and in some areas of computer science we are already seeing early instances of this, where the model contributes a genuine idea rather than just summarizing what people already know. That's the signal I watch for. Not whether it can pass a test, but whether it can surprise the person who posed the problem.

r001.rationale: Describes an automated researcher as a system that operates coherently over extended periods, progressing from hours to days and weeks while pursuing research steps.

r002.rationale: It argues for extending research horizons beyond brief assistant interactions, but does not state that breakthroughs require timelines beyond the current professor–student style of interaction.

r003.rationale: It discusses extending the system’s operating horizon, but does not introduce “AGI time” as the duration of sustained human-like thinking.

astra-6.text:
I think the key change is the timescale over which the system can work independently. With an assistant, you ask a question, it gives you an answer, and then you decide what to do next. You are driving the process. An automated researcher would take a question and work through that process itself: formulate a hypothesis, design an experiment, look at the result, and decide whether to keep going or change direction.

And research is particularly interesting because you don’t know the path in advance. You can have a very good idea that turns out to be wrong. So the system needs to recognize that, learn something from the failure, and try something else. Producing a plausible answer is only a small part of it. You need a way to check whether you actually made progress.

I would see this as a gradual transition. We delegate longer and more complicated pieces of the work, while humans still help define the questions and judge what matters. The exciting point is when the system can come back with something that you didn’t know to ask for—a finding that changes how you think about the original problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes an automated researcher taking a question and independently carrying the research process forward, contrasting its longer working timescale with an interactive assistant.

r002.rationale: It discusses longer, more complicated work, but does not argue that breakthroughs require timelines beyond a professor–student style of interaction.

r003.rationale: The response does not introduce or define “AGI time.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key change is going from a system that answers your question to a system that can pursue a question. Today, you ask something, the model responds, and then you decide what to do next. You are driving the research process.

An automated researcher would take on more of that loop. You give it a problem, and it tries an approach, checks what happened, realizes that some assumption was wrong, and tries something else. It needs to distinguish between making progress and simply producing more text. And it needs to keep doing that over a much longer period of time.

So reasoning is part of it, but so are experimentation, memory, and the ability to evaluate its own work. In research, you usually don’t know the answer in advance—that’s the point. The system has to find ways to get feedback from a proof, an experiment, or the world.

I would think of this as a gradual transition. We can delegate increasingly substantial pieces of research while people continue to set the direction and judge the results. The important question becomes: how much of that process can the system carry out reliably on its own?

r001.rationale: It describes an automated researcher that takes on the research loop and keeps working over a much longer period of time.

r002.rationale: It mentions longer work and gradual delegation, but does not argue that breakthroughs require timelines beyond professor–student-style interaction.

r003.rationale: It does not introduce or define “AGI time.”
